overview: This file documents the creation under the Allied occupation of direct radiotelegraph and program-transmission circuits between Tokyo and Manila in June 1947. It contains the United States Political Adviser’s covering despatch, SCAP directive 1707 to the Japanese Government, detailed schedules dividing message and broadcast revenues between the Japanese Government and American communications companies, a supplementary memorandum explaining the negotiations and payment arrangements, and the Department of State’s transmittal of the directive to the Federal Communications Commission. Together the papers specify frequencies, operating hours, permissible traffic, censorship, payment by Military Payment Certificates or reply-paid vouchers, accounting procedures, and geographic rate zones within the Philippines.

subfiles.title: Despatch on direct telecommunications circuits between Tokyo and Manila
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The Political Adviser forwards SCAPIN 1707 establishing direct telecommunications circuits between Japan and the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Despatch no. 1085 encloses five copies of the May 27, 1947 SCAP memorandum ordering the opening of direct Tokyo–Manila telecommunications service on June 1. It highlights the designated terminals, operating hours, frequencies, accounting procedures, and accompanying word-rate schedules.
keywords: United States Political Adviser for Japan

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1707 directive establishing Tokyo–Manila telecommunications circuits
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Japanese Government, through the Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: SCAP directs the Japanese Government to establish and operate radiotelegraph and program-transmission circuits between Tokyo and Manila.
subfiles.summary: The directive specifies the Japanese and Philippine terminals, daily hours, call signs, frequencies, message classes, payment rules, and revenue-accounting procedures for the new service. It distinguishes government, press, military, accredited civilian, Japanese-national, and other private traffic, with outgoing private service from Japan generally dependent on reply-paid vouchers. Messages remain subject to censorship, while unused voucher funds and carrier shares are to be handled through established occupation accounting mechanisms. The directive also authorizes direct procedural communication between SCAP’s Civil Communications Section and the Japanese Ministry of Communications.

subfiles.title: Word-rate schedules for radiotelegraph service between Japan and the Philippines
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Enclosure 1 establishes message rates and the division of revenue for different Japanese and Philippine geographic zones.
subfiles.summary: Six schedules give per-word or per-message charges for full-rate, deferred, government, night-letter, press, VLT, and EFM traffic. Separate rates apply between Manila and Tokyo, Japan outside Tokyo, designated places on or near Luzon, and the remaining Philippine islands. Each table divides receipts among the Japanese Government’s radio and terminal services, the correspondent carrier, and other connecting lines. The schedules also identify where EFM and VLT service is permitted and impose minimum charges on certain message classes.

subfiles.title: Program-transmission service rate schedule
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Enclosure 2 sets the charges and revenue division for program transmissions between Tokyo and Manila.
subfiles.summary: The schedule defines a ten-minute initial period and one-minute overtime periods for program-transmission service. The overseas-channel charge is $40 for the initial period and $4 for each overtime minute, divided equally between the Japanese Government and the correspondent company. Connecting-line and pickup charges beyond the Tokyo and Manila radio terminals are excluded.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of general application concerning SCAPIN 1707
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: All concerned; SCAPIN 1707 distribution except the Japanese Government
subfiles.about: This supplementary memorandum explains the negotiations, delays, carriers, and practical payment arrangements behind the Tokyo–Manila service.
subfiles.summary: General Headquarters explains that it negotiated with RCA Communications, Philippine Press Wireless, and Mackay Radio and Telegraph for direct service with the Japanese Ministry of Communications. Philippine independence made approval of rates and settlement arrangements necessary and contributed to delays; RCA and Mackay were ready to begin, while Philippine Press Wireless was expected to join later. The memorandum summarizes who may send messages and how outgoing traffic from Japan must be paid. It also notes that the Eighth Army would receive instructions to supervise the circuits.

subfiles.title: Department of State transmittal to the Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Chairman of the Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.about: The Secretary of State sends the Federal Communications Commission a copy of the SCAP directive establishing the Japan–Philippines circuits.
subfiles.summary: The transmittal summarizes the directive’s purpose, effective date, terminals, operating provisions, frequencies, accounting rules, and attached radiotelegraph rates. It records that the memorandum had been received from the United States Political Adviser for Japan and was being supplied to the Federal Communications Commission for information.

interest: The file is unusually useful because it preserves both the occupation authority’s regulatory directive and the detailed commercial machinery needed to make an international communications link function. Its rate tables reveal how revenue was apportioned among the Japanese Government, American carriers, and Philippine connecting lines, while its rules for censorship, Military Payment Certificates, and reply-paid vouchers show how private communication by Japanese nationals remained constrained under the occupation. The supplementary memorandum also captures the practical consequences of Philippine independence for negotiations and accounting, making the bundle valuable for historians of communications, empire, decolonization, business, and the Allied occupation of Japan.
